references.text: Isaiah prophesies about the great meal the Lord will prepare for all peoples on the mountain – an eschatological feast vision that forms the background for the idea of 'eating bread in God's kingdom' ([ref:Jes 25:6|Isaiah 25:6]).

Jesus speaks of Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and all the prophets in God's kingdom, where people will come from all corners of the earth and sit at the table – the eschatological meal in God's kingdom ([ref:Luk 13:28-29|Luke 13:28-29]).

As a direct response to the statement in verse 15, Jesus tells the parable of the great banquet, where the invited guests refuse the invitation and others are brought in instead ([ref:Luk 14:16-24|Luke 14:16-24]).

At the last meal, Jesus says he will not eat the Passover meal or drink from the fruit of the vine until it is fulfilled in God's kingdom – a direct link between the meal and the fulfillment of God's kingdom ([ref:Luk 22:16-18|Luke 22:16-18]).
Jesus promises his disciples that they will eat and drink at his table in his kingdom – the fulfillment of the hope for the eschatological meal ([ref:Luk 22:29-30|Luke 22:29-30]).
"Blessed are those who are invited to the Lamb's wedding feast" – a beatitude that reflects the same motif: blessedness connected with the heavenly feast ([ref:Åp 19:9|Revelation 19:9]).

Jesus says that many will come from east and west and sit at the table with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven – the eschatological meal motif in Matthew ([ref:Matt 8:11|Matthew 8:11]).

The parable of the king's wedding feast in Matthew is a parallel to the parable Jesus tells right after verse 15, with the same theme of invitation to the divine feast and rejection by those invited ([ref:Matt 22:2-14|Matthew 22:2-14]).
